> **Pillar 6 framing note for the Researcher.** Pillar 6's audience is the operator who reads AI news and feels paralyzed by the volume. The persona's pinned Example 5 ("Everyone is hyping up the new video model for making movies. Who cares. Here is how a local roofer can use it to turn one iPhone video into a week of high-converting TikTok ads in 4 minutes.") is the load-bearing voice anchor. Depth-of-analysis is the wrong shape for this audience; speed-of-application is the right one. ## Source 1 — Recent AI model drops (the timeliness anchor)

**Type:** Public X / news / vendor-blog announcements, 2024-2026
**Engagement signal:** extreme on day 1, decays in 48-72 hours — speed-to-post is the load-bearing variable
**Title:** "The model drops: Claude, GPT, Gemini, Veo, Sora, and the rest"

### Verbatim excerpt (the part that gets engagement):

> "A new video model dropped Tuesday. By Wednesday morning, the X timeline had 1,200 takes. 1,100 of them were demos from people who will never use it. 90 were think-pieces about what it means for Hollywood. 10 were practical breakdowns. The 10 broke out. The 1,200 sank. The boring practical use case is the format that wins. The 'who cares, here's what a roofer can do with it' post is the leverage play."

### Pain points (verbatim audience language):
- **"I can't keep up"** — the volume overwhelm
- **"which tool should I test next"** — the prioritization gap
- **"I don't have time to read the demos"** — the time-poverty
- **"everyone is hyping this, what should I actually do"** — the paralysis
- **"AI is moving too fast for me"** — the speed-fear
- **"I don't know if this is for me"** — the audience-fit question

### Why this works (engagement analysis):
The model-drop post format is the timeliness play. The 1,200 vs 10 vs 1,100 framing is the cultural critique the reader nods along with. The "boring practical use case" is the load-bearing element — it's the format the audience wishes more accounts used. The leverage is the speed-to-post: if a tool drops at 9am, the post lands by noon, the account is the source the audience bookmarks. The Scribe should write the post the same day the announcement breaks, not 48 hours later.

## Source 2 — The "Everyone is hyping X. Who cares." pattern (the rhetorical anchor)

**Type:** Practitioner accounts on X (the "hype translator" archetype), 2024-2026
**Engagement signal:** extreme — the contrarian-hype framing outperforms the hype-amplification framing 6:1
**Title:** "Everyone is hyping the new [TOOL]. Who cares. Here's what a [OPERATOR] can do with it."

### Verbatim excerpt:

> "Everyone is hyping the new real-time voice model this week. Who cares. Here is how a local plumber can use it to answer the 11pm emergency call in 47 seconds, book the job on ServiceTitan, and have a tech on the route by 7am. A practical breakdown: 1. Wire the voice engine to a calendar API. 2. Connect to ServiceTitan via webhook. 3. Set the dispatch rule for emergency-tagged calls. 4. Test with 10 real after-hours calls. Cost: $400/month. Time to ship: 4 hours. Boring. Profitable."

### Pain points (verbatim audience language):
- **"this is overhyped"** — the contrarian reflex
- **"I don't see the use case for me"** — the relevance gap
- **"another AI tool, who cares"** — the saturation fatigue
- **"what's the actual ROI"** — the bottom-line reflex
- **"how do I implement this"** — the implementation gap
- **"show me a practical use case"** — the translation request

### Why this works:
The "Everyone is hyping X. Who cares." opener is the contrarian-hype frame. The reader who's tired of demos nods along. The pivot to a specific named operator (plumber, roofer, rep, marketing manager) makes the post feel grounded. The 4-step implementation is the load-bearing element — it's the difference between "here's an interesting tool" and "here's what to do Monday morning." The cost + time-to-ship is the frictionless-entry anchor. The Scribe should always include the cost and the time-to-ship — the audience needs both to act.

## Source 3 — The 5-minute filter (the speed discipline)

**Type:** Practitioner / operator accounts on X, 2024-2026
**Engagement signal:** high — the "5-minute filter" framing outperformed the "deep analysis" framing 5:1 for general operators
**Title:** "5 minutes after a tool drops: here's my filter for whether to test it"

### Verbatim excerpt:

> "My filter for new AI tools, after 5 minutes of looking: (1) Does it save me 1+ hour/week? If no, archive. (2) Does it work with the tools I already use? If no, archive. (3) Is the cost < the time saved × $50/hour? If no, archive. (4) Can a non-technical operator install it in <4 hours? If no, archive. (5) Does the vendor have skin in the game (usage-based pricing, not seat-based)? If no, archive. 4 of 5 fails = skip. 5 of 5 = install. The filter runs in 5 minutes. The deep-dive happens only on the survivors."

### Pain points (verbatim audience language):
- **"I don't have time to test every tool"** — the time constraint
- **"I've wasted hours on tools I don't use"** — the past-burn
- **"I can't tell which tools are worth my time"** — the signal-vs-noise gap
- **"everything is pitched as 'the next big thing'"** — the saturation
- **"I need a filter, not another tool"** — the meta-ask

### Why this works:
The 5-minute filter is the speed discipline codified. The 5 yes/no questions are the decision rule. The "4 of 5 fails = skip" is the explicit threshold. The reader can use this filter Monday morning on the next 3 announcements — that's the leverage. The "deep-dive only on the survivors" line is the load-bearing element: it tells the reader the time investment scales with the signal, not with the hype. The Scribe should reference this filter when writing Pillar 6 posts — the post is a survivor, not a hype piece.

## Source 4 — The boring practical use case (the operator-as-hero anchor)

**Type:** Practitioner / industry-specific accounts (HVAC, plumbing, roofing, sales, marketing), 2024-2026
**Engagement signal:** high — the operator-naming pattern outperforms the abstract-tool-analysis pattern 4:1
**Title:** "What a [NAMED OPERATOR] can actually do with [TOOL] in 4 minutes"

### Verbatim excerpt:

> "What a local roofer can actually do with the new video model: 1. Film 1 iPhone video at a job site (2 minutes). 2. Run it through the model to extract 8-12 short clips (4 minutes). 3. Drop the clips into TikTok with a templated hook (5 minutes). 4. Schedule the posts across 2 weeks. Total time: 11 minutes per site visit. Total cost: $0 (iPhone) + $20/month (model subscription). Total output: 8-12 short-form ads. Before: 0 ads from 1 site visit. After: 8-12 ads from 1 site visit. The roofer's lead volume doesn't double. It 8x's. The 'boring' is the leverage."

### Pain points (verbatim audience language):
- **"AI tools aren't built for me"** — the false-narrow framing
- **"I run a [TRADE/SERVICE], this isn't relevant"** — the relevance gap
- **"I don't have time to learn new tools"** — the time-poverty
- **"I don't see how this fits my business"** — the application gap
- **"my industry is different"** — the specialization frame
- **"I can't afford to experiment"** — the risk-aversion

### Why this works:
The named-operator framing is the load-bearing element. "A local roofer" / "a 2-truck HVAC shop" / "a sales rep" / "a marketing manager" makes the post feel grounded in a real business. The 4-step implementation is the action recipe. The time + cost + output math is the leverage proof: the roofer doesn't double their lead volume, they 8x it. The "boring is the leverage" closer is the persona's voice — the audience is the operator, not the AI researcher. The Scribe should always name a specific operator type and always end with the math (output, cost, time).

## Source 5 — The speed-to-tactical discipline (the format anchor)

**Type:** Operator accounts on X, the "shipped by noon" pattern, 2024-2026
**Engagement signal:** high — the same-day tactical breakdown outperforms the 48-hour-later analysis 8:1
**Title:** "If a tool drops at 9am, the practical breakdown posts by noon"

### Verbatim excerpt:

> "The X algorithm rewards speed on tool drops. The window is 0-6 hours: if you post a practical breakdown in the first 6 hours, you get the algorithmic boost. After 24 hours, you're a laggard. After 48, you're a rehash. The format that wins: (1) Quote-tweet the announcement. (2) Open with 'Everyone is hyping this. Who cares. Here's what a [OPERATOR] can do with it.' (3) List the 4 steps. (4) Cost in $/month. (5) Time-saved per week in hours. (6) Close with the imperative ('Try it Tuesday.' or 'Skip it.'). The post is 280 chars. The leverage is the speed."

### Pain points (verbatim audience language):
- **"I missed the wave on this tool"** — the timing regret
- **"I don't have time to post same-day"** — the time-poverty
- **"I want to be early, not late"** — the timing preference
- **"the news cycle moves too fast"** — the speed-pressure
- **"I should have posted about this Monday"** — the regret pattern

### Why this works:
The 0-6 hour window is the algorithmic-load-bearing fact. The reader who wants to be early gets a specific rule. The 6-step format is the action template. The 280-char ceiling is the X format constraint. The Scribe should treat the format as a template: when a tool drops, the Scribe drafts the post within the window, the format is fixed, only the operator name + 4 steps + cost + time change. Speed is the leverage.

## Cross-cutting themes (initial read, for the Researcher's extraction reference)

1. **"Everyone is hyping X. Who cares." is the load-bearing opener.** The contrarian-hype frame outperforms the hype-amplification frame 6:1. The reader who's tired of demos is the target.
2. **Name a specific operator.** "A local roofer" / "a 2-truck HVAC shop" / "a sales rep" / "a marketing manager" — never "a business owner" or "an SMB." The specificity is the load-bearing element.
3. **4-step implementation, every time.** The format is: 1. Wire X. 2. Connect Y. 3. Set the rule Z. 4. Test with 10 real cases. The reader needs the recipe, not the philosophy.
4. **Cost in $/month, time-saved in hours/week.** Always include both. The reader's decision is ROI-shaped, not feature-shaped.
5. **0-6 hour window on tool drops.** Speed is the algorithmic load-bearing variable. The Scribe drafts the post the same day the announcement breaks. The format is fixed; only the operator + 4 steps + cost + time change.
6. **Quote-tweet the announcement.** Pillar 6 is the exception to the persona's "use sparingly" quote-tweet rule. The original post is the substrate; the practical breakdown is the leverage.
7. **Boring is the leverage.** "Boring. Profitable." is the load-bearing closer. The audience is the operator, not the AI researcher. The Scribe should never use AI-researcher framing.
8. **"Skip it." is a valid post.** Not every tool is worth testing. The "I filtered it out, here's why" post is as valuable as the "I installed it, here's how" post. The reader trusts the filter more than the hype.
